cards.claim: Dr. Shirley Ann Jackson invented caller ID, touch-tone phones, and fiber optics.
cards.name: Shirley Ann Jackson
cards.receipt: First Black woman to earn a physics PhD from MIT; former NRC chair; National Medal of Science honoree. She did not invent caller ID, touch-tone phones, or fiber optics — the honors are hers, the inventions are not.

cards.claim: Lonnie Johnson, a NASA engineer, invented the Super Soaker.
cards.name: Lonnie Johnson
cards.receipt: U.S. Patent 4,591,071 (1986). The control case: the method confirms true stories too.

cards.claim: Garrett Morgan invented the traffic light.
cards.name: Garrett Morgan — Traffic Signal
cards.receipt: Morgan patented a 3-position T-signal, U.S. Patent 1,475,024 (1923). Traffic signals predated him (Lester Wire, 1912).

cards.claim: George Washington Carver invented peanut butter.
cards.name: George Washington Carver
cards.receipt: Carver developed peanut products extensively. Peanut butter predates him; he held no patent for it.

cards.claim: Philip Emeagwali invented the Internet.
cards.name: Philip Emeagwali
cards.receipt: Real honor: 1989 Gordon Bell Prize for work on the CM-2 supercomputer. The 'father of the Internet' claim is contradicted by Gordon Bell himself.

cards.claim: 'The real McCoy' comes from Elijah McCoy — buyers demanded the genuine article.
cards.name: Elijah McCoy
cards.receipt: McCoy's 50+ patents are real (lubricator, U.S. Patent 129,843, 1872). The phrase's origin has no evidence either way — so nobody wins this claim. Best-sourced argument wins the bonus.

cards.claim: Garrett Morgan invented the gas mask.
cards.name: Garrett Morgan — Safety Hood
cards.receipt: Morgan patented a safety hood, U.S. Patent 1,113,675 (1914). Breathing apparatus predated him (Haslett, 1849).

cards.claim: Lewis Latimer invented the light bulb's carbon filament.
cards.name: Lewis Latimer
cards.receipt: Latimer patented a carbon-manufacturing process, U.S. Patent 252,386 (1882). Edison's team and Swan precede him on the filament.

cards.claim: Madam C.J. Walker invented the hot comb.
cards.name: Madam C.J. Walker
cards.receipt: The hot comb predates her. Her documented record is bigger: entrepreneur, innovator, and builder of a hair-care empire.

cards.claim: Benjamin Banneker built the first American clock — he invented it.
cards.name: Benjamin Banneker
cards.receipt: Banneker built a striking clock c. 1753, documented via Thomas Jefferson. The 'first in America' claim is unprovable.

cards.claim: Otis Boykin invented the pacemaker.
cards.name: Otis Boykin
cards.receipt: Boykin's precision resistors, U.S. Patent 2,972,726 (1961), were used in pacemakers. He did not invent the pacemaker.

cards.claim: Granville Woods, 'the Black Edison,' invented the third rail and dozens more.
cards.name: Granville Woods
cards.receipt: Woods held dozens of real railway-telegraphy patents. Some attributions on circulating lists are inflated — the verdict corrects the list, not the man.

cards.claim: Henry Sampson invented the cell phone.
cards.name: Henry Sampson
cards.receipt: Sampson himself denied it while alive. The claim traces to a circular citation web — and his record carries his own denial.
cards.verdictNote: No verdict word was published for this case in CTL-DR-TECH-001's 12-case table; the pilot deck prints only 'MYTH.' The stamp therefore shows MYTH, never FALSE.

cards.name: White City — Construction, c. 1905
cards.claim: What's being built here — and on what street?
cards.receipt: The entrance of White City amusement park, on 63rd Street, photographed under construction c. 1905. Photo: Chicago Daily News, Public Domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Register CTL-MEDUSA-CHI-000001-001, held CLEARED in the Cited Photo Archive.

cards.name: White City at Night, 1916
cards.claim: Same place as the construction card — eleven years later. What is it, and what year?
cards.receipt: White City at night, 1916 — the built park in operation, paired against the c. 1905 construction shot: two evidence cards, one entity, a decade apart. Photo: Chicago Daily News, Public Domain. Register CTL-MEDUSA-CHI-000001-002, CLEARED.

cards.name: The Trianon Ballroom, 1924
cards.claim: Name this room.
cards.receipt: The Trianon Ballroom, as its 1924 postcard sold it. Photo: postcard, publisher unknown, Public Domain. Register CTL-MEDUSA-CHI-000001-003, CLEARED. Honest limit, as published: the evidence card does not state a street address for the Trianon, so the game does not claim one.

cards.name: Bus Riders on 63rd Street, 1973
cards.claim: Which street — and which year?
cards.receipt: Riders using bus transportation on 63rd Street, 1973, photographed by John H. White for the U.S. EPA DOCUMERICA project. Photo: Public Domain, via National Archives / Wikimedia Commons. No register ID is published on this record — cited by archive title and record date, as published.

cards.name: 63rd Street, July 1973
cards.claim: Same street, same year as the bus card. What can this photo actually prove?
options: The street's documented state in July 1973
That the golden-age story is verified
cards.answer: The street's documented state in July 1973
cards.receipt: The photo documents the street in July 1973. Why it changed is a separate claim, graded separately — and parts of that story are not yet verified (see the Story Check cards). Photo: John H. White, EPA DOCUMERICA, National Archives, Public Domain. Register CTL-MEDUSA-CHI-000001-005, CLEARED.

cards.name: Whose Camera? — 63rd Street, 1973
cards.claim: You've seen his street all night. Whose camera is this?
cards.receipt: John H. White — Blacks using bus transportation on 63rd Street, Chicago, 1973, for U.S. EPA DOCUMERICA. Photo: Public Domain, via Wikimedia Commons. No register ID is published on this record — cited by archive title and record date, as published.

cards.name: Story Check — The Golden Age
cards.claim: Everybody knows it: 63rd Street's golden age made it Chicago's second-busiest commercial district. Settled fact — Myth or Record?
cards.receipt: The 63rd Street dossier itself flags this one: the commercial golden-age narrative rests on credible but single or conflicting sources — plausible and widely repeated, not yet verified. The pilot kit marks the exact per-claim grade TO MINE from the full package, so this card plays as a bonus only, never as a settled answer.

cards.name: Story Check — The Sears Date
cards.claim: The Sears on 63rd Street opened in 1929. Everybody agrees on the date — Myth or Record?
cards.receipt: The dossier names this anchor date — Sears, 1929 vs. 1934 — as resting on conflicting sources. A disputed date is played as disputed: bonus round, best-sourced argument wins, nobody settles it by voting.
